summary.text: Tikhon Belavin is remembered for his episcopal service in North America and as Patriarch of Moscow during revolution and persecution. The published life traces his early formation, pastoral ministry, and final years. It lists several commemorations, which should not be collapsed into a single calendar date. This profile uses the April 7 entry and keeps that published convention visible.

blocks.text: Tikhon was born Vasily Belavin in 1865 into a rural priest’s family. He studied in Pskov and Saint Petersburg and taught before his episcopal service. His North American appointment brought a Russian-trained bishop into direct contact with widely scattered Orthodox communities.

blocks.text: In America he traveled among the faithful, supported parish and monastic institutions, and helped develop conciliar participation. After returning to Russia, he was elected patriarch in 1917. Bolshevik persecution, pressure over church property, schism, and confinement made his patriarchate exceptionally difficult.

blocks.text: The OCA centennial history connects his American travels with the 1907 First All-American Sobor and its concern for expanding the mission. It also traces his election as patriarch during the upheavals of 1917 and the pressures of the revolutionary period.

blocks.text: The OCA church history describes the specific conflict that led to imprisonment in May 1922. Tikhon offered unconsecrated church treasures and voluntary donations for famine relief while resisting the seizure of consecrated vessels. The government confined him. The account records release in June 1923 after a statement of loyalty to the Soviet government, and interprets this as a difficult decision made for the Church’s survival. During his confinement, the state-supported Renovationists attempted to take over church administration. Their council in May 1923 sought to depose him, but alienated many of their own supporters.
